To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
subjects are willing to trade efficiency for equality, and they are willing to trade equality for efficiency, but they prefer efficiency to equality.

(1) subjects avoid an equal outcome if it is inefficient; (2) subjects avoid an efficient outcome if it is not equal; (3) subjects are willing to accept a Pareto inefficient outcome in favor of an outcome giving unequal payoffs, even when the inefficient outcome implies a larger payoff for the other player, and (4) subjects violate the independence of irrelevant alternates condition in their choice of bargaining outcomes.

(1) subjects avoid an equal outcome if it is inefficient, (2) subjects avoid an efficient outcome that gives equal payoffs, (3) subjects avoid a Pareto optimal outcome that gives unequal payoffs, and (4) the preference for efficiency is not independent from the preference for equality and total earnings maximiziation.

the question of how the outcome of a bargaining game depends on the trade-off between equality and efficiency.
